opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one where a lot of our older intuitions don't quite carry over.

In the pre-reasoning era, a lot of the uncertainty work was about calibration at the level of the final answer. You'd look at token probabilities, or sample the model many times and check agreement, and ask: when the model says it's 80% confident, is it right about 80% of the time? That's still useful, but once models are thinking for a while before they respond, a few things change.

First, the reasoning process itself becomes a source of signal. You can see whether the model considered alternatives, whether it flagged missing information, whether it went back and forth. That's informative, but you have to be careful, because the visible reasoning isn't guaranteed to be a faithful readout of what's driving the answer. So I'd treat it as evidence to evaluate, not ground truth about the model's confidence.

Second, and this matters a lot in a domain like health, I think the most important thing isn't a number attached to an answer. It's whether the model behaves appropriately given its uncertainty. Does it ask a clarifying question when the situation is underspecified? Does it say "this could be X or Y, and here's what would distinguish them"? Does it escalate, for example "you should get this looked at today," when the downside of being wrong is high? Those are behavioral expressions of uncertainty, and they're what actually protect people.

So, for measurement, I'd push toward evals that are grounded in realistic scenarios and graded by experts against rubrics. Experts can say: in this conversation, a good response would hedge here, seek this piece of context, and not overcommit there. Then you're measuring reliability as "does the model do the right thing under uncertainty," not just "is the final label correct."

Third, reliability needs to be measured in terms of worst-case behavior, not just averages. Reasoning models can be really impressive on average and still have a tail of confident, well-argued errors. In some ways those are more dangerous, because a long, fluent chain of reasoning makes a wrong answer more persuasive. So you want metrics like consistency across repeated samples, performance under paraphrase or slightly altered context, and specifically the rate of high-confidence errors in high-stakes settings.

And the last thing I'd say is that test-time compute gives us a new knob. You can look at how reliability scales with how long the model thinks, and whether more thinking actually reduces errors or just produces more elaborate justifications. Measuring that tradeoff, especially per domain and per risk level, is something I think the field should be doing a lot more of.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because the old toolkit doesn't quite fit anymore.

The classic framing was calibration: you ask the model a question, you look at the probability it assigns to the answer, and you check whether things it says with ninety percent confidence are actually right ninety percent of the time. That worked reasonably well when the answer came out in a single forward pass. The token probabilities were, in some loose sense, the model's belief.

Once the model reasons first, that breaks down in a few ways. The final answer's token probability is often very sharp, because the model has already convinced itself in the chain of thought. So the raw logits look overconfident even when the reasoning was shaky. The uncertainty has moved upstream, into the reasoning itself, and we're not really measuring it there.

So I'd say a few things. First, we should be measuring uncertainty at the level of the process, not just the output. Does the model consider alternatives? Does it notice when the evidence is thin? Does it change its mind when it should, and does it stop changing its mind when the evidence is actually clear? Those are behaviors you can evaluate, and they matter more to a user than a number next to the answer.

Second, I think verbalized uncertainty becomes much more important. If the model reasons and then says "I'm fairly confident, but this hinges on an assumption I couldn't verify," that statement is the thing to calibrate. And you can calibrate it the same way: collect lots of those statements, bucket them by expressed confidence, and check the hit rate. In the medical work I've done, that kind of expressed uncertainty is often what a clinician actually needs. They don't need a probability to three decimal places. They need to know what the model is unsure about and why.

Third, reliability now has a consistency dimension. If you run the same hard question five times with different reasoning paths and get three different answers, that's a signal, and it's a signal the model should be able to surface about itself. Self-consistency used to be a trick for improving accuracy. I think it's increasingly a diagnostic for honesty about uncertainty.

And then the hardest part, honestly, is that a confident-sounding reasoning trace is very persuasive to humans. A model that reasons fluently and wrongly is more dangerous than one that just blurts out a wrong answer, because the reasoning lends it credibility. So part of measuring reliability has to be measuring whether the reasoning is actually load-bearing. Does the conclusion depend on the steps shown, or is the chain of thought a post-hoc story? There's real research on that, and the answer is sometimes uncomfortable.

So, short version: measure the process, calibrate the words rather than just the logits, use disagreement across runs as a signal, and be skeptical of fluency as a proxy for correctness. We're earlier on all of that than I'd like.

astra-6.text:
I think reasoning makes this a more interesting question, because there are now two things you want to measure: how good is the answer, and does the model know when its answer might be wrong? Those are related, but they’re not the same. A model can get more capable without getting better calibrated.

One approach is to let the model reason through the problem and then assess its confidence. But you shouldn’t take a statement like “I’m 90 percent confident” at face value. You need to check whether, across many comparable questions where it expresses that confidence, it’s actually right about 90 percent of the time. And you want to check that in the setting where you’re deploying it, because calibration on one distribution doesn’t guarantee calibration on another.

You can also sample multiple reasoning attempts and look at whether they converge on the same answer. That’s useful evidence, but agreement isn’t proof: all of those attempts could share the same mistaken assumption.

Ultimately, I’d measure reliability at the level of the whole system. With a given amount of reasoning time and access to tools, how often does it succeed? When it can’t succeed, does it ask for clarification, seek more evidence, or appropriately defer? In something like medicine, recognizing that you don’t have enough information can be an essential part of giving a good answer. So the goal isn’t just more correct answers. It’s making uncertainty useful for deciding what to do next.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key shift is that we’re no longer measuring just a model—we’re measuring a whole process. The model can spend different amounts of compute, explore different approaches, use tools, and decide whether to check its work. So reliability has to be evaluated for that process, with a particular compute budget and a particular set of tools.

And I’d separate getting the answer right from knowing whether you got it right. You can improve accuracy through reasoning without necessarily improving calibration. A model might reason for longer, arrive at an incorrect answer, and become more confident in it. So we should measure both: how often does the system succeed, and when it expresses uncertainty, does that uncertainty actually predict failure?

One practical test is whether it can use uncertainty to make better decisions. If you let it abstain on some fraction of questions, does accuracy on the remaining questions go up? If you give it additional compute when it’s uncertain, does that help? Does it know when to ask a person for clarification?

I also wouldn’t treat a convincing explanation as evidence of reliability by itself. You want outcomes you can check, repeated trials, and evaluations that resemble the conditions where people will actually use the system. Ultimately, uncertainty is useful if it helps the system decide what to do next—not just if it produces a plausible confidence number.
